title: 3,500 Teachers Can’t Be Wrong: We Need Permission to Focus
author: Stuart Jr., Dave
summary: Dave Stuart Jr. argues that the most useful thing leaders can tell stressed teachers is that working repeatedly on a small handful of things is enough. He draws on more than 3,500 responses to his newsletter survey, which show educators who are highly pressured, expected to fix every social problem, and caught in a survival mode of data-chasing and strategy-hoarding PD. Much of that stress, he says, is avoidable because humans cannot do everything with excellence. He then traces how his own five-part literacy framework (argument, reading, writing, speaking, and growing character) grew out of the Common Core's 32 anchor standards, which he found too numerous to master one by one. The move of the piece is to turn a stress diagnosis into permission: a short list of priorities, pursued with increasing skill, restores a teacher's sense of doing the right work.
points: Teacher stress is driven largely by unbounded expectations and by an accountability culture of data and technique that has lost sight of the larger purpose, and much of it is avoidable.
Stuart's survey of roughly 3,500 educators is small next to the profession but consistent enough to show a pattern of pressure, impossible standards, and blame when a student is not reached.
Because nobody can do all things well, the wise response is to commit to a handful of repeated priorities rather than a new set of strategies every year.
His framework narrowed a long standards list to five recurring habits (argue, read, write, speak, grow character) so a teacher could judge a week of lessons by whether students practiced them.
Telling teachers 'you're okay' is framed not as lowering the bar but as restoring the nobility of the work and relieving daily anxiety.
quotes: Those last words, especially, are important: “You’re okay.” Not in the sense of “average” or “mediocre”; I’m talking about “You don’t need to feel like you’re not doing a good enough job every day.

Teachers feel that they are expected to solve all of society’s problems, every kid at a time. All of their students are to be well-fed, on grade level, and flourishing by March, no matter what. If the teacher isn’t reaching a student, then she must not be using the latest strategy or technique correctly; it’s her fault.

I think there are very few folks in education who operate out of ill motives; the majority of us teachers, administrators, and coaches live in a perpetual Survival Mode that leads to ill-thought decisions, data for data’s sake, hours studying evaluation rubrics, and “Let’s learn 1,000 strategies this year” approaches to PD. We have no sight of Everest; we’ve given it up long ago, trusting, instead, that data and technique and bureaucracy will somehow take us to the mountaintop.

But here’s the good news; this is my point: it is still possible for teachers, teams, and whole schools and districts to stand firmly on the timeless truth that humans cannot do all things with excellence, and that it is therefore wise to focus on a few things.

While the 32 anchor standards were helpful to me, there were still too many of them — far too many skills for my students and me to master through a standard-by-standard approach. We could probably “hit” them all, but we’d become excellent at none of them.

I was hitting not just the most important standards from any list, but I was hitting life’s standards. And every day, rather than shoving down a stomach-full of anxiety, I was guiding my students on a trek toward Everest, rather than a test.
